Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Fast Food Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Vignette:
Amir's eyes scan the crowded fast-food restaurant, his ears straining to filter out the cacophony of sizzling meat and chatter. It's 3 pm, the same time of day he witnessed the horrific accident at this very location three months ago. A car had careened into the entrance, injuring several customers and employees. Amir, who was working the register, had watched in horror as chaos erupted around him. Since that day, Amir has been on edge whenever he's on the job during the afternoon shift. The sound of a car horn or a loud crash from the kitchen sends his heart racing, transporting him back to the moment when everything seemed to freeze. His manager's criticism about his speed in taking orders makes him feel like he's reliving that instant, as if his mistakes could lead to disaster. When Amir is at work, he sticks rigidly to his designated tasks, avoiding interactions with customers or colleagues whenever possible. He has come to believe that if he's not in control of every aspect of his environment, something terrible will happen. His coworkers have started to notice the change in him and have begun to avoid him as well. Away from work, Amir only feels safe within the confines of his small apartment, which he has transformed into a sanctuary. He's installed blackout curtains and soundproofing materials to block out any external stimuli that might trigger another flashback. His social life has suffered as a result; he no longer attends family gatherings or meets friends for dinner. The fear of unexpected sounds is constant. Amir can't shake the feeling that every creak of the floorboard, every bang from the neighbor's apartment, signals impending doom. He finds himself constantly anticipating delays – if his bus doesn't arrive on schedule, he assumes there's been an accident; if a friend is running late, he thinks something terrible has happened to them. Despite his best efforts to maintain this fragile sense of control, Amir's life has begun to unravel. His manager has put him on probation due to his increasing absenteeism and tardiness, and his relationships with family and friends are strained. It was only when he received a letter from HR stating that his performance would be reviewed in two weeks' time that Amir realized he needed help. Now, as he sits in the therapist's office, Amir is most afraid of being told that he'll never be able to shake off these feelings of hypervigilance. He hopes that therapy will allow him to reclaim some semblance of normalcy, to feel safe outside his apartment and to reconnect with the people who matter most to him. But for now, the sound of the clock ticking away in the therapist's office is enough to send his heart racing, reminding him that, for Amir, safety remains an elusive dream.
